title: The Killing of a Sacred Deer

commenti.body:
That scene is meant to be intentionally blackly comedic, as is most of the film.

The last thing any normal person would do to get their kids to open up to them is tell them completely dead pan, with no emotion "I jerked off my dad when I was a kid." 

It isn't really that out of place considering that literally every person in the film is a weirdo. It's just another scene that demonstrates the strange world of the film. I don't think it's meant to induce any other reaction from the viewer other, "excuse me?"

Also:

>I use to think when people would say alot of people in Hollywood are pedophiles I would just think their crazy

This films was co-written by a Greek man, directed by a Greek man, stars two Irishmen, an Australian Woman, a British girl, and a 9-year old American boy, is a co-production between Britain and Ireland. You literally could not be further from Hollywood on this film.

Been a long time since I saw this movie but an important theme to it is power roles and hierarchy. Colin Farrell and his wife are both doctors, relatively powerful people at the top of the hospital hierarchy, and even their kids kinda 'admire' or even worship them, in the way that they talk about how they want to be like them when they're older. And Farrell experienced the same hierarchical role between him and his father when he was young. 

Keoghan comes in and absolutely fucks up this hierarchy, which brings chaos into the family.

My apologies, I didn't do my research. It was shown to me by a friend, so I just assumed it was an American movie, 

Maybe I didn't get the movie as I thought, I did really enjoy the movie. I was just confused along with my friend when he said it.

Even if it was blackly comedic, I find it very weird that a movie like that just added that in with it not really adding to the plot.

I'm totally curious did you not think it was odd when the father made that comment, or did it blend well with the movie for you?

I totally understand people have different views on things, so I'm curious if im the outcast on this.

The director is European where they are less skittish on nudity. However, those art scene there has a far better tradition and nudity has come to jus be accepted as something that is suitable to express a certain rawness and captivation. As for why Yorgos did that, I watched the film once and didn't like it but I do remember it had those scenes involved. And I think it's really just the fact it's at first a dark comedy from a director with European sensibilities coupled with perhaps sociopolitical messaging which is something he does.
I'm from canada, so this makes sense. I thought the movie was a thriller/mystery, not a comedy, so maybe I was looking at this movie as a thriller instead of comedy, and that's why it seemed odd.

Not everything in a movie has to add to the plot. Sometimes lines or details are there to help add some texture to the characters, sometimes it is to create mood or tone. Lanthimos does not go for “realism” in his films, they are usually heightened and absurd representations of reality. His characters often do not speak or behave naturalistically the way you have come to expect from other movies, and the odd manner in which they behave is meant to create an uncomfortable (and often darkly funny) atmosphere that unsettles the viewer. I think you either innately “get’ this when watching them, or you don’t - and if you don’t you might struggle to connect with it. That line is I think just an example of the bizarre and unsettling tone that he likes to play with, the kind of line that shocks or amuses you because of how outrageous it is. I think he wants to poke at you a bit and get a reaction, test the limits of what is acceptable.
Yeah that’s some foreign film bullshit, they love getting all disgusting like that, it’s EDGY BRO… GETS THE PEOPLE GOING.
Well yeah it was odd, but the whole movie was weird as fuck
